title: People missed that Samson lost his strength before his hair was cut (Judges 16:20)
paragraphs: People missed that Samson lost his strength before his hair was cut (Judges 16:20)
Yes. That’s the sting in the text.
Samson’s hair was the sign of his Nazirite consecration, but the real loss happened deeper than the haircut. Judges 16:20 says:
“He awoke from his sleep and thought, ‘I’ll go out as before and shake myself free.’ But he did not know that the Lord had left him.”
That line is the tragedy.
Not the scissors.
Not Delilah.
Not even the ropes.
The Lord had left him.

His strength was never magic in his hair. His strength was the presence and power of God tied to a consecrated calling. The cut hair revealed outwardly what had already collapsed inwardly. Samson had been leaking compromise for a long time before his locks hit the floor.

That is why this story hits so hard:
you can still look the same,
talk the same,
move the same,
and think, “I’ll go out as before”—
while the anointing is gone.
But here’s what people also miss: Samson’s story does not end in disgrace alone. Judges 16:22 quietly says, “But the hair of his head began to grow again.”

That is not just biology.
That is mercy whispering.
Grace was moving before victory returned.

Samson fell through lust, pride, and presumption. Yet God was not finished writing his story. And that is the Gospel shadow here: our deepest danger is not weakness, but thinking we can live without the Lord and still have power. But in Christ, even ruined people can be restored through repentance and mercy.

So yes—Samson lost more than hair.
He lost awareness of God’s departure before he felt the full consequence of his compromise.
That is the warning.
And this is the hope:

Jesus restores what sin strips.
Jesus meets the fallen.
Jesus gives back what pride wasted—through repentance, not performance.

Don’t just ask, “Has my hair been cut?”
Ask, “Am I still walking with the Lord?”
